verification.note: Second pass against the source pages. Not yet checked by a person; shown to students as AI-checked.

title: Potato Chips Manufacturer
prompt: Your client is a national potato chips manufacturer. Their profitability has declined in the last three years. Diagnose the issue.

facts.reveal: Yes, potato procurement cost has been rising.
Market prices have gone down over the same period.
Four plants: one each in the North, South, East and West.
Mostly plant by plant, with some coordination.
About eighty operate locally near individual plants; twenty supply nationally.
Roughly fifty-fifty between local and national suppliers.
That's possible, but not the primary concern.
Yes. One plant shows a particularly sharp rise: the East plant.
Yes, the client introduced stricter quality grading two years ago.

facts.asks: When the candidate says suppliers have location-specific bargaining power

crux.statement: The client pays more while the market pays less, so the problem is how it buys, not what it buys. Many small local suppliers with no scale, short-term contracts that never pass on falling prices, location power at the East plant, and stricter grading passed through as price.
crux.clue: "Market prices have gone down." The contradiction should stop the candidate from blaming the commodity.
crux.test: Remove the falling market price and the case collapses into "potatoes got expensive". Remove the 80/20 supplier split and the scale argument has no support.

paths: Value chain → procurement → parts of procurement cost (base price, transport, losses, rejects, supplier margin) → supplier structure and contracts
Start from the plant-level variance and work back to supplier structure

wrongTurns.text: Transport (the sourcing mix has not changed)

quant.working: Derived from the given facts: each local supplier gets on average 50% ÷ 80 of spend and each national one 50% ÷ 20, so national orders are 4 times larger.
quant.answer: National orders are 4 times larger on average

answerKey: Consolidate suppliers toward fewer, scalable aggregators
Sign longer contracts to lock in falling prices
Realign the grading standard with its cost
Act on the East plant specifically

close.condition: The candidate has linked at least two of the four drivers to the rising cost.
close.prompt: Pull this all together for me.

anchors.s5: Spots procurement but explains it with the commodity price. Needs the contradiction pointed out.
anchors.s7: Uses the contradiction and finds two drivers, such as supplier fragmentation and short contracts.
anchors.s9: Spots from the 80/50 split that orders are small, asks about plant variance and contracts without prompting, and links each fix to a driver.

verifierFlags.text: The 4-times order-size check is derived, not in the source: keep or drop?
verifierFlags.decision: Keep it as an optional check the grader may reward. The interviewer does not ask for it.

verifierFlags.text: The source interviewer says "you're thinking along the right lines" before it is earned.
verifierFlags.decision: Dropped. The supplier-margin fact is only "hard to say directly".
